The famous ship that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg is the Titanic.

To understand blockchain technology, imagine a massive, shared notebook that is used to record transactions. In a traditional system, like a bank, one central authority holds the only copy of this notebook. If that central office were to lose the book, or if a corrupt employee decided to erase a line, the records would be compromised.

Blockchain is different. Imagine instead that a thousand different people around the world each have an identical copy of this same notebook. Every time a new transaction occurs, it is written into a new page in everyone’s notebook simultaneously.

Here is how the security works: If someone tries to cheat and change a past entry in their own notebook, their version will no longer match the other 999 copies. The system is designed so that the "truth" is determined by the majority. Since the other 999 people have the correct, unaltered version, the single person’s change is rejected. This makes the record immutable (it cannot be changed) and decentralized (no single person or company controls it), ensuring that the data remains secure and trustworthy without needing a central referee.
